title: സംസ്ഥാനത്ത് കനത്ത മഴ മുന്നറിയിപ്പ്: വരും മണിക്കൂറുകളിൽ തിരുവനന്തപുരത്ത് റെഡ് അലർട്ട്, ഇന്ന് മൂന്ന് ജില്ലകളിൽ ഓറഞ്ച് അലർട്ട്, ജാഗ്രത വേണം | Red Alert - timeskerala.com
article_text:
HOMEKERALAസംസ്ഥാനത്ത് കനത്ത മഴ മുന്നറിയിപ്പ്: വരും മണിക്കൂറുകളിൽ തിരുവനന്തപുരത്ത് റെഡ് അലർട്ട്,...
സംസ്ഥാനത്ത് കനത്ത മഴ മുന്നറിയിപ്പ്: വരും മണിക്കൂറുകളിൽ തിരുവനന്തപുരത്ത് റെഡ് അലർട്ട്, ഇന്ന് മൂന്ന് ജില്ലകളിൽ ഓറഞ്ച് അലർട്ട്, ജാഗ്രത വേണം | Red Alert
Amina SR
October 1, 2026 3:09 pm
FacebookXPinterestVKWhatsApp

തിരുവനന്തപുരം: സംസ്ഥാനത്ത് അടുത്ത മൂന്ന് മണിക്കൂറിൽ കനത്ത മഴയ്ക്ക് സാധ്യതയെന്ന് കേന്ദ്ര കാലാവസ്ഥ വകുപ്പിന്റെ മുന്നറിയിപ്പ്. ഏറ്റവും പുതിയ വിവരങ്ങൾ പ്രകാരം തിരുവനന്തപുരം ജില്ലയിൽ റെഡ് അലർട്ട് പ്രഖ്യാപിച്ചു. തിരുവനന്തപുരത്ത് ഒറ്റപ്പെട്ടയിടങ്ങളിൽ ഇടിമിന്നലോട് കൂടിയ ശക്തമായ മഴയ്ക്കും മണിക്കൂറിൽ 50 കിലോമീറ്റർ വരെ വേഗതയിൽ വീശിയടിച്ചേക്കാവുന്ന ശക്തമായ കാറ്റിനും സാധ്യതയുണ്ട്.(Red Alert Issued For Thiruvananthapuram Heavy Rain Warning Across Kerala)

അടുത്ത മൂന്ന് മണിക്കൂർ സമയത്തേക്ക് പത്തനംതിട്ട, ഇടുക്കി, പാലക്കാട്, മലപ്പുറം ജില്ലകളിൽ ഓറഞ്ച് അലർട്ടും പ്രഖ്യാപിച്ചിട്ടുണ്ട്. ഈ ജില്ലകളിൽ ഇടിമിന്നലോടു കൂടിയ ഇടത്തരം മഴയ്ക്കും മണിക്കൂറിൽ 50 കിലോമീറ്റർ വരെ വേഗതയിലുള്ള കാറ്റിനും സാധ്യതയുണ്ടെന്ന് അധികൃതർ അറിയിച്ചു.

കൂടാതെ കോഴിക്കോട്, കണ്ണൂർ, കാസർകോട് ജില്ലകളിൽ ഒറ്റപ്പെട്ടയിടങ്ങളിൽ ഇടിമിന്നലോട് കൂടിയ നേരിയതോ ഇടത്തരം തോതിലോ ഉള്ള മഴയ്ക്കും മണിക്കൂറിൽ 40 കിലോമീറ്റർ വരെ വേഗതയിലുള്ള കാറ്റിനും സാധ്യതയുണ്ട്. കനത്ത മഴയും ശക്തമായ കാറ്റും പ്രതീക്ഷിക്കുന്ന സാഹചര്യത്തിൽ പൊതുജനങ്ങൾ ജാഗ്രത പാലിക്കണമെന്ന് കാലാവസ്ഥാ നിരീക്ഷണ കേന്ദ്രം നിർദേശിച്ചു.

വരും ദിവസങ്ങളിൽ സംസ്ഥാനത്ത് ഇടിമിന്നലോട് കൂടിയ ശക്തമായ മഴയ്ക്ക് സാധ്യതയെന്ന് കേന്ദ്ര കാലാവസ്ഥ വകുപ്പ്. മൂന്ന് ജില്ലകളിൽ അതിശക്തമായ മഴ മുന്നറിയിപ്പായ ഓറഞ്ച് അലർട്ടും വിവിധ ജില്ലകളിൽ മഞ്ഞ അലർട്ടും പ്രഖ്യാപിച്ചു. പത്തനംതിട്ട, കോട്ടയം, ഇടുക്കി ജില്ലകളിലാണ് ഇന്ന് ഓറഞ്ച് അലർട്ട് നിലവിലുള്ളത്. ഈ ജില്ലകളിൽ 24 മണിക്കൂറിൽ 115.6 mm മുതൽ 204.4 mm വരെ മഴ ലഭിക്കാൻ സാധ്യതയുണ്ട്.

യെല്ലോ അലർട്ട്

ഒക്ടോബർ 1: തിരുവനന്തപുരം, കൊല്ലം, എറണാകുളം, പാലക്കാട്, മലപ്പുറം, വയനാട്

ഒക്ടോബർ 4: പത്തനംതിട്ട, കോട്ടയം, ഇടുക്കി, എറണാകുളം

ഒക്ടോബർ 5: പത്തനംതിട്ട, ഇടുക്കി, മലപ്പുറം

ഉരുൾപൊട്ടൽ, മണ്ണിടിച്ചിൽ, മലവെള്ളപ്പാച്ചിൽ സാധ്യതയുള്ള പ്രദേശങ്ങളിലും നദിക്കരകളിലും താമസിക്കുന്നവർ അധികൃതരുടെ നിർദേശാനുസരണം സുരക്ഷിത സ്ഥാനങ്ങളിലേക്ക് മാറി താമസിക്കണമെന്ന് സംസ്ഥാന ദുരന്ത നിവാരണ അതോറിറ്റി ജാഗ്രതാ നിർദേശം നൽകി. അത്യാവശ്യമല്ലാത്ത യാത്രകളും ജലാശയങ്ങളിലും മലയോര മേഖലകളിലുമുള്ള വിനോദയാത്രകളും പൂർണ്ണമായി

Story Summary

The India Meteorological Department has issued a Red Alert for Thiruvananthapuram for the next three hours due to heavy rain and high winds, while Pathanamthitta, Idukki, Palakkad, and Malappuram are under an Orange Alert. Light to moderate rain accompanied by gusty winds is also predicted across northern districts like Kozhikode, Kannur, and Kasaragod.

title: Maharashtra Monsoon Ends With Rain Deficit, But IMD Figures Need Clarity - urbanacres.in
article_text:
Maharashtra’s monsoon season has ended with rainfall below the seasonal average, according to a report by Loksatta – Mumbai, but the figures cited for September require clarification because they do not match one another. The report says the state recorded a 52% rainfall deficit in September and a 19% deficit for the full monsoon season from 1 June to 30 September.

The report attributes the rainfall assessment and forecast to the India Meteorological Department. It says Maharashtra received widespread rainfall in July after a weaker June, but rainfall intensity declined from August. Some parts of the state continued to receive light to moderate rain as the season ended, while the impact of stormy weather was expected to weaken from Friday.

The rainfall pattern is important for both rural and urban systems. A weak monsoon can affect water storage, drinking-water planning, agriculture and the demand placed on local administrations during the post-monsoon period. For cities, the end of the monsoon does not immediately remove water-related risks: reservoir management, groundwater recharge and the distribution of rainfall across regions remain relevant to municipal planning.

According to the report, July brought above-average and widespread rainfall because of active weather systems, providing relief after a deficient June. That improvement was not sustained in August, when rainfall again fell below average. The report further states that rainfall shortages remained substantial in parts of Vidarbha, Marathwada and several areas of Sindhudurg district in the Konkan region.

The report also links the season’s weather outlook to the influence of El Niño conditions in the Pacific Ocean and says the effects of climate change had become more pronounced. Those references are presented as part of the weather assessment cited in the report; the supplied material does not provide additional data to quantify either influence.

However, the September figures require independent clarification. The report states that Maharashtra normally receives 180.3 millimetres of rainfall in September and that 87% of the expected rainfall was recorded during the month. On that basis, the shortfall would be approximately 13%, not 52%. The report also separately describes a 52% deficit for September. It is not clear from the supplied material whether the two figures refer to different geographies, periods or calculations, or whether one figure is a reporting error.

That discrepancy matters because rainfall-deficit figures guide assessments of drought stress, water availability and relief requirements. A state-level seasonal deficit and a regional deficit can coexist, but the geographical or methodological distinction must be stated clearly for the numbers to be interpreted accurately. The supplied report does not provide that clarification.

The report says light to moderate rainfall was continuing in some parts of Maharashtra, while stormy weather was expected to weaken from Friday. Confirmation of the September deficit, the affected districts and the full-season assessment from the India Meteorological Department remains necessary before the rainfall figures can be treated as settled.

title: Northeast logs lowest southwest monsoon rainfall since 1901 — IMD - Eastern Mirror Nagaland
article_text:
GUWAHATI — The Northeast has experienced its driest southwest monsoon in 125 years, with East and Northeast India recording just 1,017.1 mm of rainfall during the June-September season, officials of the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said on Thursday.

The 2026 seasonal rainfall marks the lowest recorded for the region since the IMD's rainfall series began in 1901, highlighting an unusually significant departure from the region's typically wet monsoon pattern.

The rainfall deficit was particularly persistent across Assam, Meghalaya and Arunachal Pradesh.

According to the IMD, all three meteorological subdivisions recorded deficient rainfall in each of the four monsoon months -- June, July, August and September.

The prolonged shortfall assumes significance as the Northeast is traditionally among the country's highest-rainfall regions and remains heavily dependent on the southwest monsoon for agriculture, water resources and other economic activities.

At the national level, India also ended the four-month monsoon season below normal. The country received 759.4 mm of rainfall between June and September, making 2026 the 13th lowest monsoon season since 1901 and the fourth-lowest since 2001.

However, the rainfall deficit in the Northeast stood out against the broader national picture.

The situation did not change substantially in September despite episodes of heavy to very heavy rainfall in Assam towards the latter part of the month.

The IMD assessment indicated that these intense spells were insufficient to compensate for the cumulative seasonal deficit.

Alongside the rainfall shortfall, the region also experienced an unusually warm September. East and Northeast India recorded a mean temperature of 27.95 degrees Celsius, which was 0.74 degrees above normal.

It was the sixth-highest September mean temperature recorded for the region since 1901.

The weather outlook for October remains mixed. The IMD has forecast below-normal rainfall over most parts of the country, while some areas of East India could receive normal to above-normal rainfall.

South Asians & Diaspora

For most of the Northeast, maximum temperatures are expected to remain around normal, while minimum temperatures are likely to be normal to below normal, indicating continued variability in weather conditions as the region moves into the post-monsoon period.

title: Northeast records lowest monsoon rainfall in 125 years - Hub News
article_text:
Guwahati, Oct 1: The Northeast has recorded its lowest southwest monsoon rainfall since 1901, with East and Northeast India receiving 1,017.1 mm during June-September this year, according to the latest data released by the India Meteorological Department.

The IMD said the 2026 figure was the lowest recorded for the region in its rainfall series going back to 1901.

For Assam, Meghalaya and Arunachal Pradesh, the shortfall persisted through all four monsoon months.

The three meteorological subdivisions recorded deficient rainfall in June, July, August and September, the IMD report said.

The figures are significant for a region that normally receives some of the country’s heaviest rainfall.

At the national level too, the monsoon ended below normal. India received 759.4 mm during June-September, the 13th lowest rainfall since 1901 and the fourth lowest since 2001.

But the Northeast’s performance was more striking. The region’s 1,017.1 mm seasonal rainfall was the lowest in the 125-year record.

September did not change the overall picture. Although Assam experienced heavy to very heavy rainfall on some days towards the end of the month, the spells were not enough to offset the seasonal deficit.

The region also recorded a warmer September. East and Northeast India had a mean temperature of 27.95°C, 0.74°C above normal and the sixth-highest September mean temperature since 1901.

The weather pattern could remain uneven in October. The IMD expects below-normal rainfall over most parts of the country, while some areas of East India may receive normal to above-normal rainfall. Most of Northeast India is expected to see normal maximum temperatures and normal to below-normal minimum temperatures.

India’s 2026 southwest monsoon 4th-lowest since 2001; Telangana rainfall deficit hits 17%
India’s 2026 southwest monsoon 4th-lowest since 2001; Telangana rainfall deficit hits 17%
India’s 2026 southwest monsoon was the fourth-lowest since 2001 and 13th-lowest since 1901
By Rajeswari Parasa
Published on : 1 Oct 2026 10:54 AM

Representative Image 

Hyderabad: Call it a climate emergency, Telangana recorded a 17 percent rainfall deficit this monsoon. Andhra Pradesh rainfall shortfall crossed the normal threshold to hit 29 percent.

This comes as India’s 2026 southwest monsoon was the fourth-lowest since 2001 and 13th-lowest since 1901. The monsoon ended with 759.4 mm of rainfall, 87% of the long-period average (LPA).

Telangana in normal range

While the country as a whole was in the deficient rainfall category, Telangana ended the season in the normal category, despite receiving less rain than its usual average.

The difference comes down to how the India Meteorological Department (IMD) defines rainfall categories. “Normal” does not mean a state received exactly its average rainfall. A state can record a deficit and still be classified as normal if the shortfall remains within the normal range.

Telangana recorded 615.5 mm of rainfall against its normal 740.6 mm during the southwest monsoon, a 17% deficit.

September rains become savior

The season also saw considerable swings. June and parts of the following months were relatively dry, while rainfall improved towards the end of September. The IMD recorded a major wet spell in the final week of September, with the weekly rainfall departure reaching +49% in Telangana

That late-season rain was significant for Telangana. The IMD recorded heavy to very heavy rainfall over Telangana during September 22-29, following the movement of a deep depression across the region.

Andhra Pradesh: Deficit crosses normal threshold

Andhra Pradesh, however, finished the southwest monsoon in the deficient category. The state's rainfall deficit was about 29%.

The late September weather systems did bring substantial rain to Andhra Pradesh. The IMD said a deep depression crossed the north Andhra Pradesh-south Odisha coast near Kalingapatnam on September 23, producing heavy to very heavy rainfall over Coastal Andhra Pradesh.

However, heavy rain over a few days did not necessarily erase a deficit accumulated over four months.

India: Fourth-lowest monsoon since 2001

Meanwhile, India received 759.4 mm against an LPA of 868.6 mm, leaving the country with a 13% shortfall and placing the season in the deficient category.

The 759.4-mm total was the fourth-lowest since 2001 and 13th-lowest since 1901.

Rainfall was also uneven across the country. Central India received 97% of its LPA, which was within the normal range, while the South Peninsula received only 76% and East and Northeast India 74%.

The monthly figures explain why the season ended on a weak note. June received just 65% of LPA, July recovered to 101%, August fell to 84%, and September stood at 92%.

Of the 741 districts assessed, 282 districts (38%) recorded deficient rainfall, while another 34 (5%) recorded large deficient rainfall. At the other end, 312 districts had normal rainfall, 90 had excess, and 16 had large excess rainfall.

title: Weather Alert: राजस्थान में मॉनसून की विदाई, आज बारिश का अलर्ट नहीं; दक्षिण भारत और पूर्वोत्तर में तेज बारिश की चेतावनी - samacharnama.com
article_text:
Business
Weather Alert: राजस्थान में मॉनसून की विदाई, आज बारिश का अलर्ट नहीं; दक्षिण भारत और पूर्वोत्तर में तेज बारिश की चेतावनी
By Sachin Kumar BhargaveOct 1, 2026, 14:38 IST 

देश में मॉनसून की विदाई का दौर जारी है। 1 अक्टूबर 2026 को राजस्थान के लिए मौसम विभाग ने किसी तरह की चेतावनी जारी नहीं की है। IMD के अनुसार पश्चिमी और पूर्वी राजस्थान में आज से अगले कई दिनों तक कोई मौसम चेतावनी नहीं है। राजस्थान के ज्यादातर हिस्सों में मौसम शुष्क रहने का अनुमान है। मौसम केंद्र जयपुर के अनुसार राज्य में मॉनसून की वापसी तेजी से आगे बढ़ रही है। पिछले दिनों जयपुर, टोंक, उदयपुर और बीकानेर सहित कुछ इलाकों में हल्की से मध्यम बारिश दर्ज की गई थी, लेकिन अब बारिश की गतिविधियां कम होने की संभावना है। 

राजस्थान में अगले दिनों कैसा रहेगा मौसम

मौसम विभाग के ताजा अपडेट के मुताबिक राजस्थान में 1 से 7 अक्टूबर तक पश्चिमी और पूर्वी दोनों हिस्सों के लिए कोई चेतावनी नहीं है। ऐसे में प्रदेश के अधिकांश इलाकों में मौसम साफ और शुष्क रहने की संभावना है। दिन के तापमान में बढ़ोतरी भी देखने को मिल सकती है।

दक्षिण भारत में भारी बारिश का अलर्ट

दूसरी ओर दक्षिण भारत के कई राज्यों में बारिश का दौर जारी रहने वाला है। केरल, तमिलनाडु, कर्नाटक और पुडुचेरी के कुछ हिस्सों में भारी बारिश की संभावना जताई गई है। तमिलनाडु के कुछ जिलों में तेज हवाओं और गरज-चमक के साथ बारिश हो सकती है। 

पूर्वोत्तर राज्यों में भी बारिश

पूर्वोत्तर भारत के कई राज्यों में भी मौसम सक्रिय रहने की संभावना है। नागालैंड, मणिपुर, मिजोरम और त्रिपुरा में भारी बारिश की चेतावनी है। इसके अलावा असम, मेघालय और अरुणाचल प्रदेश में भी बारिश और गरज-चमक की गतिविधियां देखने को मिल सकती हैं। मौसम विशेषज्ञों के अनुसार उत्तर भारत में मॉनसून की विदाई के साथ मौसम धीरे-धीरे शुष्क होने लगा है। राजस्थान में भी बारिश का दौर कमजोर पड़ रहा है और आने वाले दिनों में साफ मौसम रहने की संभावना है। वहीं दक्षिणी और पूर्वोत्तर राज्यों के लोगों को बारिश और तेज हवाओं को लेकर सावधानी बरतने की सलाह दी गई है।

title: ​Odisha Records Highest July Rainfall in 126 Years as State Crosses 600 mm Mark - Pragativadi
article_text:
Odisha has recorded its highest July rainfall in 126 years of documented history since 1901, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has officially confirmed.

​For the first time since record-keeping began, the state crossed the 600 mm precipitation threshold in the month of July, registering a historic 627.3 mm of monthly rainfall.

​Smashes Historical Records

​The current season’s July figure surpasses every previous high-rainfall July recorded in the state over the last century:

Year Recorded July Rainfall (mm) 2026 627.3 mm (All-Time High) 2009 586.0 mm 2001 584.2 mm 1994 552.7 mm 2014 496.2 mm 1944 491.4 mm 1932 474.7 mm 1928 468.8 mm

Driven by 10 Weather Systems Across 42 Days

​According to IMD data, the unprecedented deluge was propelled by intense and consecutive atmospheric low-pressure formations over the region. Odisha experienced the impact of 10 distinct weather systems during the active monsoon window, which collectively affected the state for nearly 42 days and produced a cumulative seasonal tally of 1,057.8 mm.

​The active atmospheric formations included:

​2 Deep Depressions

​3 Depressions

​2 Well-Marked Low Pressure Areas

​3 Low Pressure Areas

​The steady influx of these Bay of Bengal systems maintained continuous rain bands across both coastal and interior districts throughout the month.

title: Odisha Monsoon 2026 Ends With Excess Rainfall: Check Complete Details, Watch - KalingaTV
article_text:
Odisha Monsoon 2026 Ends With Excess Rainfall: Check Complete Details, Watch
Odisha Records 29% Excess Rainfall during 2026 Monsoon Season
By Himanshu Last updated Oct 1, 2026
 Share

Bhubaneswar: The 2026 monsoon rainfall season has come to an end in Odisha, with the state recording significantly higher rainfall than normal this year. Between June 1 and September 30, Odisha received 29 per cent more rainfall than the seasonal average. Odishatourism guide

According to data from the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Odisha normally receives 1,150.2 mm of rainfall during this period. However, the state recorded 1,484.3 mm of rainfall this year.

Despite the overall surplus, weather remained largely dry across the state on the final day of the monsoon season. Only one location in Nabarangpur district recorded rainfall, measuring 4 mm.

Among the districts, Boudh recorded the highest departure from normal rainfall. The district received 70 per cent more rainfall than normal, placing it in the “large excess” category.

Similarly, 22 districts recorded excess rainfall, while seven districts received normal rainfall during the season. Malkangiri, Nabarangpur, Kalahandi, Rayagada, Gajapati, Ganjam and Jharsuguda were among the districts that recorded rainfall in the normal category.

A series of weather systems over the Bay of Bengal contributed to the higher rainfall across Odisha. According to the weather department, a total of 10 weather systems developed during the monsoon season. These included six low-pressure areas, three depressions and one deep depression.

Interestingly, Odisha had recorded a rainfall deficit of nearly 47 per cent by the end of June. However, persistent rainfall during July and August helped wipe out the deficit.

By the end of August, the state had already surpassed its normal seasonal monsoon rainfall, eventually ending the season with a 29 per cent surplus.

title: Odisha Hit By 10 Weather Systems In Monsoon, Records 1,057.8 MM Rainfall - Ommcom News
article_text:
Bhubaneswar: Odisha experienced the impact of as many as 10 weather systems during the current monsoon season, according to data from the India Meteorological Department (IMD).

According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD) data, these systems affected the state for nearly 42 days and resulted in 1,057.8 mm of rainfall. The systems comprised two Deep Depressions, three Depressions, two Well-Marked Low Pressure areas, and three Low Pressure areas.

IMD’s records show that these systems occurred across July, August, and September, keeping monsoon activity vigorous over the state for a cumulative period of about 42 days and contributing substantially to the seasonal rainfall total during the affected period.

In July, Odisha received rainfall from three weather systems. A depression from July 1 to 6 brought 213.9 mm of rain, followed by a well-marked low-pressure area from July 15 to 18 that yielded 103.9 mm. A deep depression between July 25 and 29 contributed 163.4 mm of rainfall.

In August, Odisha recorded rainfall from five weather systems. A low-pressure area from August 8 to 10 brought 73.8 mm of rain, followed by a depression from 12 to 15 August that yielded 56.3 mm. Another depression between August 16 and 18 contributed 60.6 mm. A subsequent low-pressure system from August 23 to 25 delivered 78.3 mm, while a well-marked low-pressure area from August 29 to 31 added 54.4 mm of rainfall.

In September, Odisha recorded rainfall from two weather systems. A low-pressure area from September10 to 12 brought 68.8 mm of rain, while a deep depression from September 22 to 26 delivered 184.4 mm of rainfall.

Goa’s monsoon deficit has turned the 2026 rainfall season into more than a weather anomaly. The state received 2,055.4 mm of rain between June 1 and September 30, against a normal 3,007.8 mm, leaving a shortfall of nearly 32%, according to data cited by the India Meteorological Department. The result is described by IMD Goa director Nahush Kulkarni as the driest monsoon season in five decades and the state’s largest seasonal rainfall deficiency in the 1980–2026 dataset.

For a state whose settlements, farms, water systems and landscapes are shaped by a concentrated southwest monsoon, the significance of the deficit lies not only in the total rainfall lost. It is also in the timing of the shortfall. Goa’s monsoon normally provides the bulk of the annual water recharge over four months. When the season begins late, July underperforms and dry spells extend through the peak rainfall period, the state has less time to recover even if later months bring rain.

The 2026 season delivered approximately 952.4 mm less rainfall than normal. The figure is substantially higher than the deficits recorded in the other major low-rainfall years listed in the IMD dataset: 29% in 2006, 23% in 1986, 21% in 2015 and 19% in 2018. On the basis of the data cited in the report, 2026 therefore represents the largest seasonal departure from normal rainfall in Goa during the period under review.

That historical comparison is important because Goa has also experienced several recent years of excess rainfall. The state recorded 40% excess rainfall in 2020, 5% excess in 2021, a 9% deficit in 2022, 12% excess in 2023, 47% excess in 2024 and 4% excess in 2025. The sequence shows how quickly the state’s water and drainage conditions can move between surplus and shortage. A high-rainfall year may create flooding and drainage stress, while a deficient year can put pressure on water availability and recharge. The infrastructure challenge is therefore not simply to manage more rain or less rain, but to absorb large variations between the two.

The IMD’s explanation for this year’s deficit points to disruptions in the early and middle stages of the southwest monsoon. In June, the formation of a cyclone or severe cyclone over the South China Sea drew moisture towards the Bay of Bengal and delayed the onset of the monsoon, Kulkarni told the Times of India. He also said the jet streams were not strong enough to push southwest winds towards the west coast and the Indian subcontinent.

The delayed onset mattered because it reduced the time available for the season to build its normal rainfall total. But the more consequential weakness came in July, which is usually Goa’s peak monsoon month. According to the IMD account, July recorded deficient rainfall and included a prolonged dry spell of around 10 days. Kulkarni said that when July does not perform well, it becomes difficult to make up the deficit in August and September. Both of those months also recorded insufficient rainfall this year.

This pattern exposes a central feature of monsoon-dependent urban systems: seasonal totals can conceal operational stress. Two years may receive similar rainfall totals but produce very different outcomes depending on when the rain arrives, how long dry spells last and whether rainfall is intense enough to generate runoff rather than recharge. The supplied data does not establish the effect of this year’s deficit on individual reservoirs, aquifers, municipal supply systems or agricultural output. It does, however, establish that the shortfall was distributed across the season and that the peak rainfall month also underperformed.

For cities and towns, the immediate institutional question is how rainfall data is translated into water planning. A monsoon deficit of nearly one-third can affect the amount of water entering surface storage and groundwater systems, but the article does not provide storage levels or official drought classifications. Nor does it report restrictions, supply interruptions or emergency measures. Those absences matter: the rainfall figure indicates a heightened water-security concern, but it cannot by itself show the precise condition of each local water system.

The same distinction applies to urban flood management. Goa’s recent excess-rainfall years demonstrate that drainage systems must often be designed for intense rainfall, even as water managers prepare for prolonged dry periods. This is a difficult planning balance. Drainage capacity is usually judged by how quickly stormwater can be moved away from roads and built-up areas, while water security depends on retaining and recharging as much usable water as possible. The source report does not assess whether Goa’s existing systems are meeting either objective, but the contrast between the state’s recent rainfall surpluses and the 2026 deficit makes the tension clear.

The institutional responsibility is also distributed. The IMD measures and explains rainfall patterns. State and local authorities manage water supply, storage, drainage, land-use decisions and public responses. The supplied report does not identify any new state policy or municipal intervention linked to the deficit. That means the current development is primarily a warning signal from the weather record rather than evidence of a completed policy response.

The longer rainfall series cited by the IMD provides a useful baseline for that signal. The previous largest seasonal deficit in the dataset was 29% in 2006. The 2026 shortfall is nearly three percentage points greater, while the rainfall total is 952.4 mm below normal. In practical terms, the comparison places this year outside the recent pattern of moderate deficits and excess seasons described in the report.

At the same time, the data should not be used to claim that one deficient monsoon establishes a permanent shift in Goa’s climate. The supplied material does not provide a long-term climate attribution study, a trend analysis beyond the rainfall comparisons, or projections for future seasons. What it does show is a substantial departure from normal rainfall within a state where the monsoon is central to water replenishment and where rainfall conditions have varied sharply in recent years.

That distinction is relevant for urban planning. If authorities treat a deficient year only as an exceptional weather event, the immediate focus may remain on seasonal supply management. If they treat the wider sequence of excess and deficit years as a planning challenge, the question becomes how water, drainage and land-use systems can operate under greater variability. The report itself does not answer that policy question, but its figures make the question unavoidable.

The next formal milestone cited by the IMD is the expected withdrawal of the monsoon by October 10. Until then, the state’s final seasonal position will remain tied to the remaining rainfall and the timing of withdrawal. The evidence currently confirms an unprecedented deficit within the supplied historical comparison, a weak July and insufficient rainfall in August and September. It does not yet establish the condition of Goa’s reservoirs, groundwater, municipal networks or agricultural systems. Those indicators will determine how a record-low monsoon translates into an urban and public-service challenge beyond the rainfall statistic.

title: Bihar Weather बिहार में बाढ़ का कहर, लेकिन आगे कैसा रहेगा बिहार का मौसम? - Deshaj Times
article_text:
- Advertisement - ज़्यादा जानें समाचार भौगोलिक संदर्भ समय और कैलेंडर

Bihar Weather: नेपाल से लगातार आ रहे पानी और नदियों के उफान ने बिहार में आम जनजीवन को मुश्किल में डाल दिया है। राज्य के 6 जिलों में करीब 1.59 लाख लोग बाढ़ से प्रभावित हुए हैं। गंडक और कोसी समेत कई प्रमुख नदियां खतरे के निशान से ऊपर बह रही हैं। इसी बीच, मौसम विभाग (IMD) ने आज यानी गुरुवार के लिए बारिश से थोड़ी राहत मिलने की संभावना जताई है। हालांकि, बारिश रुकने के बाद उमस से लोगों की परेशानी बढ़ सकती है।

- Advertisement -

बिहार में बाढ़ का कहर: तटबंध टूटे, मकान बहा

नदियों के बढ़े जलस्तर से तटबंधों पर दबाव लगातार बढ़ रहा है। बगहा और बेतिया में चार जगहों पर तटबंध टूटने की जानकारी मिली है, जिससे निचले इलाकों में पानी तेजी से फैल रहा है। कई घरों में पानी घुस जाने से लोगों को सुरक्षित स्थानों की तलाश में निकलना पड़ रहा है। प्रशासन की टीमें स्थिति पर लगातार नजर बनाए हुए हैं।

- Advertisement -

छपरा के हजलपुर गांव में बाढ़ की भयावह तस्वीर सामने आई है। यहां पानी के तेज बहाव में एक पूरा मकान देखते ही देखते ढह गया और नदी में समा गया। इस घटना से आसपास के ग्रामीणों में दहशत का माहौल है। तेज बहाव के कारण निचले इलाकों में रहने वाले लोगों की मुश्किलें और बढ़ गई हैं।

- Advertisement -

पटना, बेगूसराय और खगड़िया में गंगा नदी का जलस्तर भी लगातार बढ़ रहा है। पटना में कई घाट गंगा के पानी में डूब गए हैं, जिससे तटीय इलाकों में बाढ़ का खतरा मंडरा रहा है। लोगों को सतर्क रहने की सलाह दी जा रही है।

मौसम विभाग ने आज के लिए कोई अलर्ट जारी नहीं किया है।

आज बारिश से मिलेगी राहत, पर उमस बढ़ाएगी परेशानी

बाढ़ के मौजूदा हालात के बीच मौसम को लेकर राहत भरी खबर सामने आई है। गुरुवार को बिहार में भारी बारिश की कोई संभावना नहीं है। मौसम विभाग ने आज किसी भी जिले के लिए कोई विशेष अलर्ट जारी नहीं किया है। दिन में धूप निकलने से अधिकतम तापमान में 2 से 3 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक बढ़ोतरी हो सकती है। हालांकि, हवा में नमी अधिक होने के कारण उमस भरी गर्मी लोगों को परेशान कर सकती है।

मौसम वैज्ञानिकों के अनुसार, मॉनसून की गतिविधि अब कमजोर पड़ गई है। राज्य के ऊपर फिलहाल कोई मजबूत मौसमी सिस्टम सक्रिय नहीं है, जिससे बारिश की गतिविधियों में कमी आने की उम्मीद है।

किन जिलों में हुई सामान्य से अधिक बारिश?

पिछले 24 घंटों के दौरान राज्य के 13 जिलों में सामान्य से अधिक बारिश दर्ज की गई। इसमें खगड़िया में सबसे ज्यादा बारिश हुई, जो सामान्य से 474 फीसदी अधिक थी।

जिला (District) बारिश (मिमी) (Rainfall (mm)) टिप्पणी (Remark) खगड़िया 36.2 सामान्य से 474% अधिक मुंगेर 29 सामान्य से अधिक लखीसराय 24.7 सामान्य से अधिक भागलपुर 19.8 सामान्य से अधिक बेगूसराय 19.2 सामान्य से अधिक रोहतास – सामान्य से अधिक बांका – सामान्य से अधिक अरवल – सामान्य से अधिक गोपालगंज – सामान्य से अधिक औरंगाबाद – सामान्य से अधिक सीवान – सामान्य से अधिक पश्चिम चंपारण – सामान्य से अधिक मधेपुरा – सामान्य से अधिक गया – सामान्य से अधिक सहरसा – सामान्य से अधिक शेखपुरा – सामान्य से अधिक जमुई – सामान्य से अधिक नालंदा – सामान्य से अधिक पटना – सामान्य से अधिक वैशाली – सामान्य से अधिक

यह आंकड़ा दर्शाता है कि कुछ क्षेत्रों में हुई भारी बारिश ने बाढ़ की स्थिति को और गंभीर बना दिया है, जबकि अन्य क्षेत्रों में सूखे जैसे हालात हैं।

सीमांचल में बारिश की कमी और कुल मॉनसून घाटा

एक तरफ जहां कुछ जिलों में सामान्य से अधिक बारिश हुई, वहीं दूसरी ओर सीमांचल और उत्तर बिहार के कुछ जिलों में बारिश की भारी कमी देखी गई।

जिला (District) बारिश (मिमी) (Rainfall (mm)) सामान्य से कम (Less than Normal) अररिया 2.7 79% किशनगंज 3.9 सामान्य से कम पूर्णिया 4.4 सामान्य से कम कटिहार 9.6 सामान्य से कम शिवहर – सामान्य से काफी कम सीतामढ़ी – सामान्य से काफी कम मुजफ्फरपुर – सामान्य से काफी कम दरभंगा – सामान्य से काफी कम

मॉनसून सीजन में अब तक बिहार में कुल 678.9 मिमी बारिश दर्ज की गई है, जबकि इस अवधि में सामान्य बारिश 992.8 मिमी होनी चाहिए थी। इस हिसाब से राज्य में अब तक सामान्य से 32 फीसदी कम बारिश हुई है, जो चिंता का विषय है।

आगे कैसा रहेगा बिहार का मौसम?

मौसम विभाग के पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार, 1 और 2 अक्टूबर को बिहार में मौसम सामान्य रहने की संभावना है और इन दिनों के लिए कोई विशेष चेतावनी जारी नहीं की गई है। हालांकि, 3 से 6 अक्टूबर के बीच राज्य के कुछ हिस्सों में मौसम का मिजाज बदल सकता है। इस दौरान गरज-चमक के साथ तेज हवाएं चलने की संभावना है, जिसके लिए लोगों को सतर्क रहने की जरूरत है।
